deep.reconstruction: This is the opening of Euler's 1757 Berlin memoir (published 1759) on the buckling of columns. Euler recalls the rule he derived in the elastica supplement (Additamentum I, 'De curvis elasticis') of the Methodus inveniendi (1744). The rule concerns a prismatic column, 'equally strong along its whole length', i.e. of constant flexural rigidity. Let a be the height and Ekk the 'moment du ressort', which is the flexural rigidity EI in modern terms. The largest load the column can bear without bending is then P = π²·Ekk/a². So the critical load varies inversely as the square of the height. Euler announces that he will explain how to obtain Ekk in practice. In §II he makes a conceptual point: Ekk is not a property tied to elasticity, i.e. to the body's power to restore itself after bending. It measures resistance to bending, so it might better be called the 'moment de roideur' (moment of stiffness). It therefore applies to any body that resists flexure, elastic or not. On the next page he applies this mainly to wooden columns. He also gives an experimental way to find Ekk: clamp the column at its base, apply a small horizontal force F at the top, and measure the top deflection δ. Then Ekk = F·L²(L/(3δ) − 1/2) ≈ F L³/(3δ), which is the modern cantilever relation δ = FL³/(3EI). The problem served is the practical estimation of column strength, i.e. Euler buckling plus measurement of bending stiffness.
errors: Possible end-condition / factor-4 inconsistency. The 1744 Additamentum treats a column fixed at the base and free at the top, and gives a critical load of π²Ekk/(4a²) for a column of height a. The rule quoted here, π²Ekk/a², is the value for a column of length a with both ends hinged, or equivalently for a cantilever of height a/2. The column used for measuring Ekk on the next page is clamped at the base and free at the top. If the quoted rule were applied to such a column, it would overstate the load by a factor of 4 unless the end conditions are specified. From this page alone I am unsure how Euler resolves this later in the memoir.
The bracketed correction term −1/2 in F·AC²(AC/(3Dδ) − 1/2) comes from the finite-deflection expansion in §39 of the 1744 supplement. Euler rightly drops it, since it is negligible for small Dδ.

ideas.what: Critical (buckling) load of a prismatic column proportional to flexural rigidity divided by length squared, P = π²EI/L²
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1744 Additamentum; E238 of 1757/59; E508 etc.)
ideas.where_published: Methodus inveniendi (E65), Additamentum I; Sur la force des colonnes (E238); later column papers (e.g. E508)

ideas.what: Rigidity Ekk as resistance to flexure, independent of whether the body is restoring (elastic) or not; renamed 'moment de roideur'
ideas.modern_name: Flexural rigidity / bending stiffness EI (not tied to elasticity)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler; the conceptual history is discussed by Truesdell (1960)
ideas.where_published: E238 §II; discussed in Truesdell, Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera omnia II 11-2)

ideas.what: Experimental determination of EI from the tip deflection of a clamped column under a horizontal tip force, Ekk ≈ F L³/(3δ) (developed on the next page)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (1744, §39 of the elastica supplement); also Daniel Bernoulli and others in the elastica tradition

deep.surprise_reason: This is a well-known memoir in the history of buckling, thoroughly covered by Truesdell. The only point of note is the end-condition/factor-4 subtlety in the quoted rule, which historians already discuss. Nothing here appears new or uncredited.
